title: Northstar Fintech - Console cost reporting / usage insights demo
summary: Redwood demoed in-console usage insights focused on cost/usage breakdown by API route and model, with drilldowns and export workflow. Northstar asked detailed questions about reconciliation vs invoice totals (rounding, time windows, late events), RBAC/role-based access to cost views and exports, and audit logging for downloads. Redwood clarified attribution semantics (fallbacks/retries, cache hit/miss, streaming overhead), data freshness indicators, and planned CSV export + shareable report controls. Next steps include sending the export column spec, confirming RBAC mapping for Northstar’s roles, and scheduling a follow-up for security/audit requirements and billing reconciliation tolerance.
topics: Route + model cost breakdown (tokens in/out, cache, retries, fallbacks)
RBAC: who can view cost vs usage; workspace-level cost visibility setting
Export (CSV) flow, signed URLs, and audit logging requirements
Data freshness/lag indicators and late-arriving events
Private/VPC considerations and data residency questions
next_steps: Redwood to send Northstar the draft CSV export column list + rounding rules and an example export.
Northstar to share their internal roles/permission matrix (FinOps vs Eng vs Security) for mapping to Redwood RBAC.
Redwood to confirm audit log fields for export/download events and provide a sample audit event payload (sanitized).
Schedule a 30-min follow-up focused on reconciliation methodology (invoice vs console totals) and acceptable tolerance policy.
action_items: Markus Klein: Email Northstar export format spec + sample CSV (by EOW).
Evan Scott: Provide overview of RBAC gating for cost views and export permissions + recommended defaults (by EOW).
Jenna Wu: Send Northstar security requirements for audit logging and retention controls (next 3 business days).
Priya Nair: Provide an example invoice line-item breakdown they want to reconcile to (next week).
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Northstar Fintech - Console cost reporting / usage insights demo
Date: 2026-01-21
Time: 15:03 ET
Duration: 48 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood) - Solutions Engineering
- Evan Scott (Redwood) - Solutions Engineer
- Priya Nair (Northstar) - FinOps
- Samir Desai (Northstar) - Platform Engineering
- Jenna Wu (Northstar) - Security
- Owen Hart (Northstar) - Engineering Manager

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, I think we’re recording. Cool. Thanks everyone for joining. The goal today is to show you what we’re building around in-console usage insights—cost and usage broken down by API route and model—and then spend most of the time on your questions, especially reconciliation and permissions.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Sounds good.

[00:20] Samir Desai: Yep.

[00:22] Evan Scott: Hey all.

[00:24] Markus Klein: Quick agenda: 10-ish minutes walkthrough, then we’ll go deep on billing consistency, RBAC, export, and audit logging.

[00:35] Owen Hart: Great.

[00:38] Markus Klein: Okay I’m sharing my screen. Let me know if you can see the Redwood Console.

[00:43] Priya Nair: Yep, we see it.

[00:45] Markus Klein: Cool. So this is under Usage, then Cost Insights. We’re in a beta environment right now. The primary view is a table: rows are normalized route, model family/version, and then we show total cost, tokens in, tokens out, cache hit rate, average latency, and then a few “drivers” columns.

[01:07] Samir Desai: When you say normalized route, is that like /v1/chat/completions vs the full path?

[01:13] Markus Klein: Exactly. For OpenAI-compatible endpoints it’s usually stable. For customer custom routes, we template path parameters so you don’t get cardinality explosion—like /v1/projects/{project_id}/… becomes a canonical form.

[01:28] Samir Desai: Okay.

[01:30] Markus Klein: If you click into a route, you can drill down by model, and you can also flip the pivot: model first then routes. And filters across the top: time range, workspace/project, environment, region, deployment mode.

[01:45] Priya Nair: Deployment mode meaning hosted versus dedicated?

[01:48] Markus Klein: Yep, hosted API, Dedicated, and for some accounts Private/VPC. In your case you’re mostly Dedicated in us-east, right?

[01:56] Samir Desai: That’s the plan, yes.

[01:58] Markus Klein: So here’s a drilldown. Notice this banner up top: “Data last updated 12 minutes ago; some events may arrive late.” That’s our freshness indicator. It matters for reconciliation, and we can talk about how we treat late events.

[02:15] Jenna Wu: Is that based on your warehouse job, or is that real time?

[02:19] Evan Scott: It’s based on the aggregation pipeline. We ingest metering events continuously, but the interactive view is backed by an aggregated dataset, so it’s near-real-time but not streaming-by-second.

[02:32] Markus Klein: Now, the “Top cost drivers” panel on the right—this is early but the idea is to show “what changed” week-over-week. Example: token out increased 28%, cache hit rate dropped from 42 to 18, retries increased, model mix shifted. Each is clickable and links to docs or recommended levers.

[02:52] Priya Nair: I like the “what changed” framing. For finance, we need consistent totals. That’s like the first gating item.

[03:00] Markus Klein: Totally. Let’s jump into that. Before that, I’ll show export quickly. There’s Export CSV. In beta we’re doing async exports for large ranges so the UI doesn’t hang. You can download or generate a share link depending on your role.

[03:17] Jenna Wu: Share link… that sounds like something we’d want to control tightly.

[03:21] Evan Scott: Yep, it’s behind permissions. Also we plan to log it like any other sensitive action—download initiated, download completed, actor, workspace, filters.

[03:33] Markus Klein: Okay. That’s the high-level. Let’s stop the tour and go into your questions.

[03:41] Priya Nair: Yeah, let’s do reconciliation. If I pull “last month” in console, will it match invoice? And what do you mean by match—like to the penny?

[03:52] Markus Klein: Great question. Our target is consistent totals versus billing for the same time window and scope. There are a few reasons you might see minor drift: rounding at different levels, timezone cutoffs, and late-arriving events that get attributed into the correct day after the fact.

[04:12] Priya Nair: Okay, but how do you define the time window? Our invoice uses UTC and closes at midnight UTC.

[04:18] Evan Scott: We support timezone selection in the UI, but the canonical billing windows are UTC. For reconciliation we recommend using UTC in the console and the exact invoice period.

[04:29] Samir Desai: What about if you’re showing daily buckets—do you bucket by request start time or completion time?

[04:36] Evan Scott: For metering, it’s based on event time at the gateway—effectively request completion for token accounting because we need token out. But the underlying “session” can span seconds; it’s typically within a minute anyway. The main thing is we’re consistent across the billing hook and the insights aggregation.

[04:57] Priya Nair: So your billing system and this console view use the same events?

[05:02] Markus Klein: That’s the intention. The billing line items are derived from metering events. The insights view is aggregated off the same feed, with some extra dimensions. But there’s a reconciliation check job to ensure totals match within a defined tolerance.

[05:19] Priya Nair: What tolerance? Like 0.1%?

[05:22] Markus Klein: We’ve been using a “small absolute” tolerance for rounding differences on small accounts, and percentage-based for larger totals. I don’t want to quote a hard number without confirming the current policy, but think “pennies to low dollars” at normal volumes, not like thousands.

[05:40] Priya Nair: Okay. We’ve seen vendors say that and then it’s off by 2% because of rounding or cache accounting.

[05:47] Markus Klein: Yeah, understood. The cache topic is important: we show cache hit/miss for transparency, but billing is based on billed tokens under your pricing rules. If cache reduces tokens processed, it affects cost. If a customer has a special contract where cache is priced differently, we need to make sure the insights “cost” aligns to the billing rules.

[06:11] Samir Desai: Can you break out “billed tokens” vs “raw tokens”? Like tokens in/out vs tokens processed after caching.

[06:18] Evan Scott: In the dataset we track tokens in/out, and we also track cached-prefix savings where available. The UI can show both; for beta we’re prioritizing “billed cost” as the primary number and tokens as explanatory metrics.

[06:34] Priya Nair: Good. Because finance won’t care if tokens out is high unless it moves the invoice.

[06:40] Markus Klein: Exactly. The “cost” column is meant to tie to invoice totals. The drivers explain why cost moved.

[06:49] Jenna Wu: On reconciliation—what about retries and fallbacks. If your system retries a request, are we billed twice? And does the route breakdown show it as two requests?

[06:59] Evan Scott: Good question. There are multiple “retry” concepts. Client-side retry from your app: that’s two separate requests and it’ll show as such. Redwood internal retry—say a transient GPU error and we retry within the request lifecycle—our policy is to not double-charge for failed attempts when we can confidently mark the final outcome. For insights, we track retry count as a driver metric, but cost should reflect what’s billed.

[07:24] Jenna Wu: And fallbacks? Like if you failover to a compatible model.

[07:29] Markus Klein: For fallbacks, attribution is to the model that actually served the completion. We also keep a “requested model” field, so you can see if policy-based fallback was happening. That’s one of the “what changed” signals.

[07:45] Samir Desai: That’s useful. We had a bad day with another provider where it silently shifted models.

[07:50] Markus Klein: Yep, exactly the kind of thing we want visible.

[07:56] Priya Nair: Okay, but the invoice—does it list fallback model or requested model?

[08:01] Evan Scott: The invoice line items typically correspond to the billed model. We can confirm how it would show for your contract. But for internal chargeback, the requested model can be helpful.

[08:14] Owen Hart: From an engineering perspective, I want to see what routes are expensive. Like “/v1/chat/completions with llama 70B” versus “embeddings”. Do you show route plus model together?

[08:27] Markus Klein: Yep, that’s the main table. Route + model. Then you can drill into context length distribution and streaming overhead.

[08:37] Owen Hart: Streaming overhead—what’s that exactly?

[08:40] Markus Klein: For streaming responses, there’s some additional per-request overhead and sometimes tokenization/flush patterns affect how quickly tokens go out. We don’t charge “extra” for streaming per se, but streaming workloads often correlate with longer sessions and more output tokens. In the drivers, we try to show if a route shifted from non-streaming to streaming and that’s correlated with cost.

[09:05] Priya Nair: So just to be super clear: you’re not adding some “streaming fee”.

[09:09] Markus Klein: Correct. The cost is based on tokens and your pricing. The streaming metric is diagnostic.

[09:18] Jenna Wu: Switching to RBAC. Who can see cost? We have a strong separation: engineers can see usage metrics but not dollars; only FinOps and limited managers can see actual spend.

[09:31] Evan Scott: We support that. There’s a workspace setting to “hide cost” for non-finance roles. You can still show tokens, request counts, latency. Then finance roles can toggle cost view.

[09:44] Jenna Wu: Is that an org-level setting or per workspace/project?

[09:48] Evan Scott: Per workspace, and you can inherit from org defaults depending on your enterprise config. Also the specific permissions are tied to roles—like “Billing Viewer” versus “Developer”.

[10:02] Priya Nair: We would want a “FinOps viewer” that can export. And engineering managers maybe can see cost at high level but not export.

[10:10] Evan Scott: That’s doable. Exports are a separate permission from viewing cost. Same for shareable links.

[10:17] Jenna Wu: And is there audit logging for those actions? We need that for SOC controls.

[10:22] Markus Klein: Yes. For export we generate an audit event. It includes actor, time, workspace, filters, and file size. For share link, we log creation and access.

[10:36] Jenna Wu: When you say “access”, do you mean every download is logged?

[10:40] Evan Scott: Yes, for signed downloads we can log when the link is redeemed. There are some nuances if a browser prefetches, but generally we log download start and completion.

[10:52] Jenna Wu: Okay. Also retention—how long are those audit logs retained?

[10:57] Markus Klein: Depends on your plan, but for enterprise we can align to your retention requirements. We’ll confirm specifics.

[11:05] Priya Nair: Back to export. If I export route+model breakdown for 30 days, can it time out?

[11:11] Markus Klein: In beta we’ve seen 30-day interactive queries get heavy depending on cardinality. That’s why export is async and we’re adding query optimizations. Practically, we recommend using weekly or 14-day ranges for interactive and use export for longer.

[11:28] Samir Desai: Cardinality meaning like if routes are un-templated?

[11:31] Evan Scott: Exactly. If someone sends a route with an ID in the path and we don’t normalize it, you can end up with thousands of unique routes. We have guardrails: normalization library, plus a fallback bucket like “/unknown” or “/untemplated” until we can map it.

[11:49] Samir Desai: For OpenAI-compatible endpoints, we have /v1/responses and /v1/chat/completions. Will those show distinct?

[11:56] Markus Klein: Yes, they’ll show as distinct canonical routes. Also we can group at a higher level (“chat” vs “embeddings”), but the primary is route-level.

[12:08] Owen Hart: I want to ask about “per environment”. We have staging and prod; can we filter and compare?

[12:15] Markus Klein: Yes, env is a filter and a dimension in the dataset. You can compare if you export or use the “compare to previous” mode.

[12:26] Priya Nair: The big issue: invoice ties to contract pricing—discounts, committed spend, maybe different rates by model tier. Can the console show those rates or is it a generic MSRP cost?

[12:40] Markus Klein: Good catch. The console “cost” should reflect your actual billed cost under your contract, not list price. We’ll confirm your specific pricing model. For beta accounts, we’re validating that the “effective rates” match billing.

[12:57] Priya Nair: Okay. If you’re applying credits, like promotional credits or commit burn-down, does that show too?

[13:04] Evan Scott: In the first version, the route/model breakdown is “usage cost” pre-credit. We can show “net billed” in a separate billing view. For reconciliation, we can map both.

[13:17] Priya Nair: That matters. Finance cares about net.

[13:21] Markus Klein: Understood. Most teams want both: engineering wants unit economics drivers; finance wants net invoice. We’re working on making the totals consistent and then adding clear labels.

[13:36] Jenna Wu: When engineering can’t see cost, can they still see “top drivers” text that mentions percentages? Like “cost up 20%” would leak.

[13:45] Evan Scott: Good point. The UI can adapt. For restricted roles it can say “usage up” in tokens and requests, and omit dollar amounts. We’ll take that as a requirement.

[13:58] Jenna Wu: Please.

[14:00] Markus Klein: Yep, noted.

[14:03] Samir Desai: On the reconciliation job you mentioned—how often does it run? And what happens if it detects drift?

[14:11] Evan Scott: We run it daily and for some windows more frequently. If drift exceeds threshold, we alert internal on-call and we can show a banner in the UI if the data is partial or under investigation.

[14:26] Samir Desai: That’s good. We had a vendor where it just silently was wrong.

[14:31] Markus Klein: Yeah, we’d rather be transparent.

[14:36] Priya Nair: Can we download a report and share it with auditors? Like a link that expires, with access logs.

[14:44] Evan Scott: That’s basically the shareable report feature. It would be a signed URL with expiration. Access is gated by auth, and we audit.

[14:54] Jenna Wu: Must require login. No public links.

[14:57] Evan Scott: Yes, login required.

[15:01] Owen Hart: I’m curious about the “drivers” list—are you going to give recommendations like “use batching”?

[15:07] Markus Klein: It’ll be lightweight: “token out increased; consider stricter max_tokens, use JSON mode for structured outputs, review prompts.” For cache: “enable prefix caching” where applicable. For routing: “pin model version” or “use smaller model for this route”. But we’re not automatically changing anything.

[15:29] Owen Hart: Fine. Just links are good.

[15:31] Priya Nair: How do you calculate cost by route when a request spans multiple internal calls? Like tool calls, function calling, whatever.

[15:40] Evan Scott: We attribute based on the user-facing API route that initiated the generation. Internal tool calls still sit within that request. If you have multiple calls from your app, those show as separate requests.

[15:54] Priya Nair: Okay.

[15:56] Samir Desai: Are you capturing request IDs that we can cross-reference? Like if a cost spike happens, can we trace a few examples.

[16:04] Markus Klein: In the console, yes, there’s a trace link if you have tracing enabled. For the cost table, we won’t list request IDs (too many), but drilldown can show top exemplars.

[16:17] Samir Desai: Got it.

[16:19] Priya Nair: One more billing nuance: currency and rounding. Our invoice is USD, two decimals. Are you rounding per request or per line item?

[16:29] Evan Scott: We avoid rounding per request in the aggregation; we store high precision and round at presentation/export. The invoice might round at a different stage depending on the billing system. That’s one source of small drift; the reconciliation job accounts for that.

[16:47] Priya Nair: Okay. I’d want to see the exact rounding rules documented.

[16:52] Markus Klein: We have a draft export spec that includes rounding and currency. We’ll send it.

[16:58] Jenna Wu: Audit event fields—can you include IP address and user agent? That’s a common control request.

[17:05] Evan Scott: For console-initiated downloads we can capture IP and user agent. For API-based export downloads, similarly. We’ll confirm what’s already included and what we can add.

[17:19] Jenna Wu: Okay.

[17:22] Markus Klein: We should also cover data residency quickly. You’re primarily US-based. Do you need that the analytics data stays in-region?

[17:30] Jenna Wu: Yes, ideally. Also who can access it internally.

[17:35] Markus Klein: For Dedicated/VPC we can keep telemetry and aggregated datasets within allowed regions depending on the deployment. Access is restricted; we have audit logs and role separation. We can set up a security review session for deeper detail.

[17:54] Jenna Wu: We will need that.

[17:56] Priya Nair: Back to the UI: can I do “top routes by cost” and export just top 50?

[18:02] Markus Klein: Yes, table sorting and an export option that respects current filters/sort. There’s also pagination.

[18:12] Priya Nair: And can I filter by model family? Like llama-3.1 vs mistral.

[18:17] Evan Scott: Yes, we have model family and version bucketing. It’s important for aliases—if a model name changes, it still maps to a stable family.

[18:29] Samir Desai: Aliases—can that cause duplicates in exports?

[18:33] Evan Scott: It can if the alias mapping changes over time and we don’t backfill correctly. We’ve seen that in early tests. The plan is to enforce stable keys and optionally show “display name” separate from “bucket key.”

[18:50] Priya Nair: Good.

[18:52] Owen Hart: Can you show me an example “what changed” card? Like what it says.

[18:56] Markus Klein: Sure. Here’s one: “Route /v1/chat/completions increased cost +34% vs previous week. Primary drivers: tokens_out +29%; cache_hit_rate down 18 points; model mix shifted toward llama-3.1-70b (+12%).” And then it has “view details.”

[19:18] Owen Hart: Okay.

[19:20] Jenna Wu: Again, if engineers can’t see dollars, that copy should not say cost.

[19:25] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ll make it role-aware.

[19:28] Priya Nair: On exports, do you have an API endpoint or only UI?

[19:33] Evan Scott: Both. The UI calls an export endpoint. You can also call it via API to generate CSV for ingestion into your BI tool. It’s an export job lifecycle: create job, poll status, get signed download URL.

[19:50] Priya Nair: Nice. Then we can automate.

[19:53] Samir Desai: What about rate limits or throttling so someone doesn’t export huge files constantly?

[19:59] Evan Scott: We have throttles and size limits. Also permission gating.

[20:05] Markus Klein: If a job is too large, we’ll ask to narrow filters or switch to a coarser time bucket.

[20:13] Priya Nair: Time buckets—hourly vs daily?

[20:16] Markus Klein: In beta, daily and hourly for shorter ranges. For long ranges, daily. For interactive, we default to daily.

[20:27] Priya Nair: Okay.

[20:29] Samir Desai: I have another question about late events. If events arrive late and you reconcile after the month is closed, does the console change historical numbers? Because finance hates numbers changing after close.

[20:43] Evan Scott: Great point. We treat “closed billing periods” as stable once invoiced. For insights, we can still correct data if there was a bug, but we can also expose a “data finalized” marker per period and avoid changing totals unless necessary. For late events, the billing system already has a cutoff; we align with that for invoice. For operational views, we can keep updating the last few days.

[21:10] Priya Nair: That’s important. We need a story: after invoice, numbers are locked.

[21:14] Markus Klein: Agreed. We’ll capture that requirement.

[21:18] Jenna Wu: Also, who can change the “hide cost” setting? That needs to be admin-only.

[21:25] Evan Scott: Yes, workspace admin or org admin only.

[21:29] Jenna Wu: Great.

[21:31] Markus Klein: Anything else on security?

[21:34] Jenna Wu: SSO and role mapping. We do SAML groups. Can you map “FinOps” group to cost viewer.

[21:41] Evan Scott: Yes, we support SSO role mapping. We can map groups to roles.

[21:48] Jenna Wu: Okay.

[21:50] Owen Hart: I’d like to make sure route normalization works for our internal gateway. We wrap your SDK and sometimes the route is “/api/chat” not “/v1/chat/completions”.

[22:02] Markus Klein: If your app calls your own internal endpoint and then calls Redwood, we’ll see the Redwood API route, not your internal. But if you’re proxying and preserving your route in headers, we can optionally ingest a “customer route” tag—within limits.

[22:20] Samir Desai: That might be nice but careful on cardinality.

[22:23] Markus Klein: Exactly. In initial release, we stick to Redwood canonical routes.

[22:29] Priya Nair: For finance chargeback, canonical routes might be enough.

[22:34] Markus Klein: Okay.

[22:36] Priya Nair: Can you show per-project? We have multiple product lines.

[22:41] Evan Scott: Yes, project is a first-class dimension if you send the project/workspace identifier with requests. Most customers do.

[22:50] Samir Desai: We do, yes.

[22:52] Markus Klein: Great.

[22:55] Priya Nair: I’m going to ask the annoying question: why can’t we just use AWS Cost Explorer for this.

[23:01] Markus Klein: Not annoying. AWS sees infrastructure spend but not “route + model + tokens out.” They won’t know that /v1/chat/completions is driving spend because of high output tokens or cache misses. We’re trying to attribute at the application interface level.

[23:20] Priya Nair: Fair.

[23:21] Samir Desai: Another competitor question: OpenAI gives some usage dashboards. We need route-level.

[23:28] Markus Klein: Exactly. Most dashboards are model-level. Route-level is the missing piece when multiple teams share one account.

[23:38] Jenna Wu: And with RBAC, hopefully.

[23:41] Markus Klein: Yep.

[23:43] Priya Nair: Okay, so next steps. We need docs: export columns, rounding, reconciliation method, and RBAC matrix.

[23:52] Markus Klein: Yep. We’ll send the draft export spec and a sample. Evan can share a short RBAC overview. For reconciliation, we can do a follow-up session with one of our billing folks, but I can at least send our current policy.

[24:10] Evan Scott: And for audit logs, we can send a sample audit event with the fields.

[24:15] Jenna Wu: Perfect.

[24:17] Owen Hart: When is beta available for us?

[24:21] Markus Klein: We can add you to the allowlist once we confirm the roles and you’re okay with beta limitations. Likely within a week.

[24:31] Priya Nair: What are limitations.

[24:33] Markus Klein: Mainly: long time range queries can be slower; some drivers are heuristic; and we may adjust labels. But totals should align, and if not we want to know.

[24:46] Priya Nair: Okay.

[24:48] Samir Desai: Can we pilot with one workspace first.

[24:51] Evan Scott: Yes.

[24:53] Markus Klein: Great.

[24:55] Jenna Wu: I’ll send our role mapping needs and audit requirements.

[25:00] Markus Klein: Sounds good. Anything else before we wrap?

[25:05] Priya Nair: One last thing: if we export and load into Snowflake, are there stable IDs for route and model, or just display names.

[25:14] Evan Scott: There will be stable keys for route normalization and model bucket, plus display names. That’s in the export spec.

[25:23] Priya Nair: Great.

[25:25] Markus Klein: Alright. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up with those materials and schedule the reconciliation + security follow-up.

[25:33] Owen Hart: Thanks.

[25:34] Jenna Wu: Thank you.

[25:35] Samir Desai: Thanks.

[25:36] Priya Nair: Bye.

---

Questions captured:

- How are timezones and time windows handled (UTC vs local)?
- How are retries, fallbacks, and streaming represented and billed?
- Can engineering be restricted from seeing dollar values while still seeing usage metrics?
- What audit logs exist for exports and shareable links? What fields are included?

Notes:
- Customer emphasized “numbers locked after close” requirement.
- Customer requires admin-only toggles for cost visibility.
